narrative:
The model predicted a 54% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability tipped above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your LSAT score had the strongest influence and pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. At 25, it sits well below the average of 37 among students who were accepted, signaling weaker preparation in the eyes of the model. Your undergraduate GPA came next and worked in your favor, though not enough to offset the LSAT. At 3.30 it is actually slightly above the 3.23 average of accepted students, giving the model a modest reason to expect you might pass. Your third-year grades in law school ranked third. Placing in the fourth decile (compared to an average around the sixth among accepted students) added a small additional nudge toward predicting failure.

Taken together, the lower LSAT and weaker class ranking outweighed your solid college GPA, producing a prediction that you were more likely than not to fail the bar. 

What you should do next is clear: retake the LSAT and aim for a meaningfully higher score. Improving that single factor would likely change the model’s outlook and open the door to admission. Focus your preparation there, then reapply.
